newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy's Dini sees possible EMU slippage.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy's Dini sees possible EMU slippage.

text.p: Italy's Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini added his voice on Thursday to suggestions that the planned January 1999 launch date for Europe's single currency could be put back to give more countries a chance to join.

In an interview with La Repubblica newspaper, he said plans to assess aspirant countries for membership early in 1998 on the basis of their 1997 economic performance meant a year of data would not be taken into account.

"I think there will be a collective assessment to decide whether it is convenient to put the start date back slightly so that 1998 and not just 1997 can be taken into consideration as well," Dini was quoted as saying.
A senior foreign ministry official said the quoted remarks reflected Dini's view that "it would not be a drama if they put the EMU start...(back) to June or July 1999".
"This would enable us to have one more year" of data, the official told Reuters. "If this would mean more countries being in EMU, a larger EMU, this would be worthwhile."
The lira weakened slightly on the Dini comments but swiftly regained poise to stand at around 992.50 to the German mark.

Dini's interview was published as the centre-left government prepared to present a tough 1997 budget to parliament later on Thursday containing measures it hopes will slash next year's new public debt by a huge 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion).

Prime Minister Romano Prodi has insisted the budget will allow Italy to hit the low deficit target needed to enter economic and monetary union (EMU) from the start, despite scepticism from political opponents and many economists.

French President Jacques Chirac also publicly questioned Italy's fitness to join the EMU founder group on Tuesday before a threat from an incensed Prodi to scrap a bilateral summit starting in Naples on Thursday night prompted him to row back.
Dini, Prodi's predecessor as premier and treasury minister before that, said he did not believe the strict economic criteria for EMU membership laid down in the Maastricht Treaty would be softened.
"I'm not hoping for a discount, that would be a baseless hope," he said.

But he said the 1997 budget was the maximum effort Italy could make and suggested it might just miss the EMU target by saying the package would take the deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio "close" to the required three percent.
"I've read today that a senior member of the Bundesbank has suggested a delay (to the EMU launch) for all countries of one or two years," Dini said.
"That is not an idea to be shared but...you know, we aren't the only ones who are having to make a huge effort. The French have their problems as well."

Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick suggested on Wednesday that all nations should consider postponing the launch date by one or two years to give aspirants, including Germany and France, more time to prepare adequately for the union.
